summary:
Venezuela does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The age of consent is 16 and applies identically to same-sex relations. The country has no hate-crime statute and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, so violence or discrimination directed at a trans person carries no dedicated penalty or aggravating circumstance.

Legality has not prevented police action. In May 2026 the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state. Officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality', a charge with no basis in Venezuelan law.

There is no working legal gender recognition route. A 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal requires each case to be assessed individually, with certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the Tribunal has not granted the requested name and gender changes. SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people could request an identity card matching their gender identity, but no administrative procedure or mechanism exists to enact the relevant article. A trans visitor cannot expect to obtain Venezuelan documents that match their gender.

Partner recognition is partial. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, and the law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions. Lesbian couples are permitted to access IVF. A December 2016 ruling of the Supreme Tribunal of Justice allowed a baby to be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames and held that the state must protect all families without distinction.

Institutional protection is limited. The National Assembly unanimously passed a resolution in May 2016 establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia; the Supreme Court suspended that resolution in August 2016. Venezuela has marked the International Day Against Homophobia since 2000, and the government has begun participating in Pride events.

Tamara Adrián and Rosmit Mantilla were elected Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of Venezuela's legislature; Adrián had run as the country's first transgender candidate for the National Assembly. In December 2015 Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla, a Voluntad Popular deputy and the country's first openly gay parliamentarian, a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion data is mixed and dated. A Cronica Uno poll conducted on 2-3 March 2023 found a majority of Venezuelans agreeing that the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% recognised the term LGBTIQ+ and 13% did not, and 36% considered gay, lesbian or bisexual orientation to be innate. A 2023 Equilibrium CenDE poll found 48% supported adoption by same-sex couples (34% totally, 14% somewhat) against 39% opposed. A 2013 Pew survey found 57% of 18-29-year-olds believed homosexuality should be accepted by society, compared with 51% of 30-49-year-olds and 45% of those over 50.

Legislative movement on relationship recognition has stalled. Aporrea reported on 31 January 2014 that an equal-marriage bill was to be presented to the National Assembly that week; no later enactment is recorded.

Persecution has tracked the political crisis. Reporting in September 2024 described intensified persecution of LGBTQ Venezuelans following the disputed July 2024 election, and the opposition presidential candidate left the country on 7 September 2024.
localsOnly:
For residents seeking legal gender recognition, the 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal sets an individual assessment standard: certified birth certificates plus a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity. No name or gender change has been granted under it.

Identity documents remain unchanged. SAIME's September 2016 announcement that transgender people may request an identity card matching their gender identity has no implementing administrative procedure or mechanism.

Family law: same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. The Supreme Tribunal of Justice ruled on 15 December 2016 that a baby may be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames, basing the decision on Article 75 of the Constitution and declaring that the state must protect all families without distinction, so that children and teenagers born into same-sex families enjoy all the rights and guarantees of children born into opposite-sex families. Lesbian couples may access IVF. The law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal remains unresolved: no ruling granting the requested name and gender changes is recorded.

Whether an administrative procedure has since been created to implement SAIME's September 2016 identity-card announcement is not sourced.

The fate of the equal-marriage bill reported in January 2014 after its presentation to the National Assembly is not recorded, and whether the August 2016 suspension of the 17 May resolution remains in force is not sourced.

Two reference compilations are catalogued as sources: the EUAA country focus on Venezuela, covering the period through 2025, and the October 2024 LGBTQ guide published by AFS and the Vance Center. Their individual findings are not itemised separately here.
